text: In October of twenty ten, Falcon Reservoir on the Rio Grande was completely full. One hundred percent.
Thirteen years later, in October of twenty twenty-three, it was down to just eight percent, tied for its lowest level in more than three decades. Today, it sits at about twenty-three.

Almost every faucet, field, and factory in the Lower Rio Grande Valley depends on this river and on two reservoirs upstream. And the Valley is growing fast: new subdivisions, new plants, a rocket company building next door.
So for anyone who builds, buys, or lends here, the question is simple. Will there be enough water to grow? The answer is more surprising than you might think. This is RGV News.

The Valley's water starts far upstream. Two big reservoirs on the Rio Grande, Amistad near Del Rio and Falcon below Laredo, store the supply that flows down to the Valley's cities and irrigation districts.
In Brownsville, about seventy percent of the city's water comes from the Rio Grande. Across the Valley, the river is the backbone of the supply for cities and farms alike.

Those reservoirs are shared with Mexico. And under a treaty signed in nineteen forty-four, Mexico owes the United States a share of the water from its rivers that feed the Rio Grande, counted over five-year cycles.

For years, Mexico fell behind. When the last cycle closed in October of twenty twenty-five, it ended deep in debt. In early twenty twenty-six, after pressure from Washington, Mexico committed to deliver at least three hundred and fifty thousand acre-feet a year, and to repay what it owes.

This October, the first year of the new cycle closed, and Mexico says it met that minimum. That's real progress. But by most estimates, it still owes more than eight hundred thousand acre-feet from the last cycle.
An acre-foot, by the way, is enough water to cover a football field about nine inches deep. The state water board says that's about what six Texans use at home in a year.
Here's what the last fifteen years looked like. Both reservoirs were full in twenty ten. Then came a long drought.

In July of twenty twenty-four, Amistad hit its lowest level in at least three decades, about twenty-four percent. Falcon spent most of twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four below fifteen percent.
This fall brought some relief. Amistad has climbed back to about fifty-three percent, and Falcon to about twenty-three. Better than a year ago. But nowhere near healthy.
So here's the surprising part. When water gets short in the Valley, cities are not first in line to lose it.
The water rights system in the Amistad-Falcon reservoir system protects municipal water. Irrigation rights are the ones that get cut in a drought.

The region's own twenty twenty-six water plan says it plainly: the Valley does not have municipal unmet needs. Farms do. In a severe drought, irrigation in the region could come up short by about eight hundred and eighty thousand acre-feet a year by twenty thirty.

We've already seen what that looks like. In twenty twenty-four, the Valley's sugar mill, the last one in Texas, shut down after fifty years, citing heat and a shortage of irrigation water. Hundreds of workers were laid off. The state is now trying to revive it.
But the line between farm water and city water isn't as clean as it sounds. Across much of the Valley, water for towns travels through the same irrigation canals that serve the fields.
Raymondville, for example, still gets its Rio Grande water delivered through the Delta Lake Irrigation District. Its general manager says the district is running at a fraction of its former capacity.

And those canals need enough water flowing through them to push deliveries down the line. The regional plan warns that as farm water rights are converted away, there's less of that push water, so more has to be diverted to get the same amount to a city's tap. That's one reason fixing the canals matters so much.
So if cities are protected, where does the water for new neighborhoods come from? Largely from farms.

As farmland becomes subdivisions, the water rights attached to that land can be converted from irrigation to municipal use. But not one for one. Under state rules, it takes about two acre-feet of irrigation rights to make one acre-foot of city water.
The regional plan expects tens of thousands of irrigated acres to give way to urban growth over the coming decades, more than ten thousand in Hidalgo County alone by twenty thirty.

For developers, that makes water a cost and a timing question. In some Valley cities, proving that a project has its own water supply is a condition of building. Others have been rethinking their rules.

In twenty twenty-four, Mission considered pausing new developments larger than five acres because of water scarcity, then stepped back at the last minute. This spring, it put a six-month pause on new car washes, citing water conservation and too many in one area, then repealed it after a lawsuit.
Meanwhile, the growth keeps coming. Edinburg says it has at least a hundred and twenty-seven subdivisions under construction, and its mayor has promised an independent water supply by twenty thirty.

The city is studying desalination of brackish groundwater, and capturing stormwater before it drains into the Rio Grande and out to the Gulf. It's also spending thirty-three million dollars to expand its wastewater treatment plant, from about twelve million gallons a day to thirteen and a half.
And in Brownsville, as we covered in our last episode, SpaceX's land deal is paying for a water reuse plant and a treatment-plant expansion. Water is now part of how big projects get negotiated.
The good news: there's real money moving to create new supply.

Statewide, Texas voters approved Proposition 4 in twenty twenty-five, about seventy percent in favor. It dedicates up to a billion dollars a year in sales tax to a new state water fund, starting in twenty twenty-seven.

Closer to home, a proposed package of up to a hundred and sixty-four million dollars would turn leaky open canals into pipelines across twelve irrigation districts, saving up to forty-four thousand acre-feet a year. Some districts are already being funded.

And on South Padre Island, a private venture is planning a billion-dollar seawater desalination plant, fifty million gallons a day. That's roughly fifty-six thousand acre-feet a year, a meaningful new source. But it would be privately owned, with the company controlling contracts and prices, and many steps remain before it breaks ground.
So what does this mean if you build, buy, or lend in the Valley?

The tap is not likely to run dry in town. Cities are protected first. The bigger risks are cost, timing, and rules: the price of new water, the rights a project may need to bring with it, and how fast cities change their development policies when the reservoirs drop.

Before you buy land or start a project, ask three questions. Who supplies water to this site, a city, a water supply corporation, or an irrigation district? Does the project need to bring its own water rights, and at what cost? And what's that supplier's drought plan when Falcon falls again?

There's an opportunity side too. Projects that come with their own water, through converted rights, reuse, or efficient design, may move faster when cities tighten up. Builders who know the water rules can spot land that others overlook, or avoid deals that look cheap until the water bill arrives.
And the money now flowing into canals, reuse plants, and desalination means construction and engineering work across the Valley for years to come, whatever the reservoirs do.
The Valley has water to grow. But it's not free, and it's not automatic. The projects that plan for water first will be the ones that pencil out. This is RGV News.
